exp_design: On-farm experiments were conducted during the 2015 and 2016 cropping seasons, with three farmers at each site, making a total of nine farmers hosting the tests. Each farm hosted one full experimental repetition, thus functioning as an experimental block. The purpose of this trial was to compare the yield responses of five CSA treatments against the recommended levels (see Section 2.2 for details) of treatment (the control).
time_raw: This study was conducted during two consecutive cropping seasons (2015 and 2016)
subpractice_description_raw: MD+LL: maize intercropped with lablab and microdosed fertilizer. Micro-dosing + maize/lablab intercropping (53,333 and  66,666 plants ha 1)
intercrop_subpractice: Intercrop (N fixing and Non N fixing)
fert_subpractice_raw: Micro-dosing + maize/lablab intercropping (53,333 and  66,666 plants ha 1)
out_exp_design: The economic feasibility of the studied practices was evaluated based  on gross margin (GM) (net returns) (CIMMYT, 1988). The GM ha 1 was calculated as the difference between total revenue and total variable costs (TVC). TVC was calculated as the sum of labour and input costs (seed and fertilizers); the latter were obtained from local markets. Total revenue was estimated as the sum of maize yield (grain and stover) and  legume biomass (kg ha 1). Revenue obtained from each crop (maize and  legume) was calculated by multiplying yields/biomass (kg ha 1) with average farm gate price recorded at each site during the two cropping seasons. Monetary values were converted to USD at the rate of USD 1.0 = Ethiopian Birr (ETB) 22.91.
product_raw: Total revenue was estimated as the sum of maize yield (grain and stover) and  legume biomass (kg ha 1). Revenue obtained from each crop (maize and  legume) was calculated by multiplying yields/biomass (kg ha 1) with average farm gate price recorded at each site during the two cropping seasons. Monetary values were converted to USD at the rate of USD 1.0 = Ethiopian Birr (ETB) 22.91.
out_subindicator_description_raw: Yields were obtained through field measurements, while information on seeds, fertilisers and labour inputs were obtained through farmer interviews and field observations with costs obtained from local markets. Total revenue was based on sum of yields of maize, stover and legume biomass. Maize yields were based on harvesting crops from 70 sq m farm section covering three random 5.63 sq m of each subplot. The average of three subplots was taken and used to compute the yield per ha for each farm.

exp_design: The experiments were laid out factorially in randomized complete block design (RCBD) with three blocks. Each block consisted of nine treatments, involving two soybean varieties (TGX 1448-2E) and (Samsoy-2), each with three maize (TZR-EW) population densities (38,000; 44,440 and 53,330 plants/ha) (2 x 3) factorial and sole crop of each soybean variety at 266,660 plants/ha and maize at 53,330 plants/ha for determining the productivity of the intercropping systems.
subpractice_description_raw: 38,000/TGX 1448-2E: maize (TZR-EW)/soybean varieties (TGX 1448-2E)
fert_subpractice_raw: Mixed fertilizer NPK was separately applied to soybean by drilling at 21 DAP to supply 10 kg N, 36 kg P2 O5 and 20 kg K2O per hectare and this was achieved by mixing 22 kg urea + 200 kg P2O5 + 100 kg K2O per ha. Also 450 kg/ha NPK (20:10:10) compound fertilizer was applied to maize stands by side dressing at the same time with soybean, that is, 21 DAP to supply 90 kg N, 45 kg P2 O5 45 kg K2O per ha as recommended by BNARDA (2000). This was achieved by mixing 450 kg NPK 20:10:10 (BNARDA, 2000).
weed_method_raw: Two manual weedings were done at three and six weeks after planting (WAP).
chem_subpractice_raw: A broad spectrum insecticide (Cypertex 10EC) was sprayed at 500 ml per 400 litres of water per hectare using an 18 L Jacto sprayer. This was to control leaf hoppers and grass hoppers, which are the devastating leaf eating insects in soybean (Onwueme and Sinha, 1991).
out_exp_design: The experiments were laid out factorially in randomized complete block design (RCBD) with three blocks x two seasons (6 samples per treatment)
authors: Muoneke, C. O., et al.

exp_design: The experiments were laid out factorially in randomized complete block design (RCBD) with three blocks. Each block consisted of nine treatments, involving two soybean varieties (TGX 1448-2E) and (Samsoy-2), each with three maize (TZR-EW) population densities (38,000; 44,440 and 53,330 plants/ha) (2 x 3) factorial and sole crop of each soybean variety at 266,660 plants/ha and maize at 53,330 plants/ha for determining the productivity of the intercropping systems.
subpractice_description_raw: 44,440/Samsoy-2: maize (TZR-EW)/Soybean variety (Samsoy-2)
fert_subpractice_raw: Mixed fertilizer NPK was separately applied to soybean by drilling at 21 DAP to supply 10 kg N, 36 kg P2 O5 and 20 kg K2O per hectare and this was achieved by mixing 22 kg urea + 200 kg P2O5 + 100 kg K2O per ha. Also 450 kg/ha NPK (20:10:10) compound fertilizer was applied to maize stands by side dressing at the same time with soybean, that is, 21 DAP to supply 90 kg N, 45 kg P2 O5 45 kg K2O per ha as recommended by BNARDA (2000). This was achieved by mixing 450 kg NPK 20:10:10 (BNARDA, 2000).
weed_method_raw: Two manual weedings were done at three and six weeks after planting (WAP).
chem_subpractice_raw: A broad spectrum insecticide (Cypertex 10EC) was sprayed at 500 ml per 400 litres of water per hectare using an 18 L Jacto sprayer. This was to control leaf hoppers and grass hoppers, which are the devastating leaf eating insects in soybean (Onwueme and Sinha, 1991).
out_exp_design: The experiments were laid out factorially in randomized complete block design (RCBD) with three blocks x two seasons (6 samples per treatment)

exp_design: We classified cattle ranches by production strategy on the basis of these practices as a surrogate measure of cattle yield. We validated this classification later by comparing methods for clearing forests and for increasing forage availability with cattle yield declared by ranchers. We collected data on cattle yield and birds on ranches with different production intensities. Measured from the perimeter, ranches with the same type of production system were at least 50 km apart. At least one ranch in every type of production system was located in each zone (premontane, umbral, and chaco) to account for variations in elevation and rainfall. To collect baseline data on birds, we surveyed forest fragments that had not been used for agriculture or intensive logging in the past 5 years, were >1000 ha, and had a canopy cover >70%. Each forest fragment was in the same zone (premontane, umbral, or chaco) of a group of 4–5 selected ranches (to which served as baseline land cover) and at a distance of 5–50 km from those ranches (measured from the perimeter). This selection process yielded a sample of 7 high-intensity pasture systems, 5 intermediate-intensity silvopastoral systems, 7 low-intensity silvopastoral systems, 8 very-low-intensity systems, and 6 forest fragments (Fig. 1).

out_exp_design: We established 6 25-m radius sites in which we conducted point counts in each of the 33 sampling sites (27 cattle ranches and 6 forest fragments). To locate survey sites, we subdivided the total area of each sampling site into a grid of 100-ha square cells (i.e., usual paddock size and shape) and established a point-count site in the center of 6 randomly selected cells.

exp_design: We classified cattle ranches by production strategy on the basis of these practices as a surrogate measure of cattle yield. We validated this classification later by comparing methods for clearing forests and for increasing forage availability with cattle yield declared by ranchers. We collected data on cattle yield and birds on ranches with different production intensities. Measured from the perimeter, ranches with the same type of production system were at least 50 km apart. At least one ranch in every type of production system was located in each zone (premontane, umbral, and chaco) to account for variations in elevation and rainfall. To collect baseline data on birds, we surveyed forest fragments that had not been used for agriculture or intensive logging in the past 5 years, were >1000 ha, and had a canopy cover >70%. Each forest fragment was in the same zone (premontane, umbral, or chaco) of a group of 4–5 selected ranches (to which served as baseline land cover) and at a distance of 5–50 km from those ranches (measured from the perimeter). This selection process yielded a sample of 7 high-intensity pasture systems, 5 intermediate-intensity silvopastoral systems, 7 low-intensity silvopastoral systems, 8 very-low-intensity systems, and 6 forest fragments (Fig. 1).
subpractice_description_raw: IISS: intermediate-intensity silvopastoral systems, stands of native trees of varying densities in which planted non-native grasses have replaced the woody understory
agrof_subpractice_raw: IISS: intermediate-intensity silvopastoral systems, stands of native trees of varying densities in which planted non-native grasses have replaced the woody understory
out_exp_design: We established 6 25-m radius sites in which we conducted point counts in each of the 33 sampling sites (27 cattle ranches and 6 forest fragments). To locate survey sites, we subdivided the total area of each sampling site into a grid of 100-ha square cells (i.e., usual paddock size and shape) and established a point-count site in the center of 6 randomly selected cells.

exp_design: We classified cattle ranches by production strategy on the basis of these practices as a surrogate measure of cattle yield. We validated this classification later by comparing methods for clearing forests and for increasing forage availability with cattle yield declared by ranchers. We collected data on cattle yield and birds on ranches with different production intensities. Measured from the perimeter, ranches with the same type of production system were at least 50 km apart. At least one ranch in every type of production system was located in each zone (premontane, umbral, and chaco) to account for variations in elevation and rainfall. To collect baseline data on birds, we surveyed forest fragments that had not been used for agriculture or intensive logging in the past 5 years, were >1000 ha, and had a canopy cover >70%. Each forest fragment was in the same zone (premontane, umbral, or chaco) of a group of 4–5 selected ranches (to which served as baseline land cover) and at a distance of 5–50 km from those ranches (measured from the perimeter). This selection process yielded a sample of 7 high-intensity pasture systems, 5 intermediate-intensity silvopastoral systems, 7 low-intensity silvopastoral systems, 8 very-low-intensity systems, and 6 forest fragments (Fig. 1).
subpractice_description_raw: VLIS: very-low intensity systems, closed forests with free-ranging cattle feeding on understory shurbs and ephemeral grasses
agrof_subpractice_raw: VLIS: very-low intensity systems, closed forests with free-ranging cattle feeding on understory shurbs and ephemeral grasses
out_exp_design: We established 6 25-m radius sites in which we conducted point counts in each of the 33 sampling sites (27 cattle ranches and 6 forest fragments). To locate survey sites, we subdivided the total area of each sampling site into a grid of 100-ha square cells (i.e., usual paddock size and shape) and established a point-count site in the center of 6 randomly selected cells.

exp_design: Based on aerial photographs from 1996 (and in some cases 1984–1985) we selected all forest patches of more than 1 km2. Of these (approximately 40), we selected 15 areas evenly distributed in the elevational range of 1700–2000 m asl. In a similar manner we selected all agricultural areas of more than 1 km2 from aerial photos from 1967, 1975, and 1984–1985. To be considered an agricultural site, the area had to have been in cultivation on the oldest available aerial photo. On the basis of this initial selection we selected 15 sites that were evenly distributed in the area and in the same elevational range as the forest sites. Finally, we selected all stands (around 20) that appeared to be exotic tree plantations (i.e., dense tree cover in an area that in the oldest aerial photos was treeless). In the field we randomly selected one tree in each of the forest sites in an area that was minimally disturbed by humans (selective logging, beehives, coffee production) and >200 m from the forest edge. In the center of the agricultural sites, we selected a mature shade tree in a home garden with coffee (in one site we found no such home garden, hence n = 14). In the plantations we selected a random tree in the middle of the stand. We selected 7 Cupressus-plantations and six Eucalyptus plantations (n = 13 exotic plantations) to get an even distribution between the two plantation types. (See Supporting Information for a list of the sites and Fig. 1 for the distribution of the sites across the investigated landscape.)

exp_design: The experiment was laid out in split-plot design with seven crop sequences in main plots, viz. maize (Zea mays)-wheat (Triticum aestivum), maize-potato (Solanum tuberosum)mentha (Mentha arvensis) + onion (Allium cepa), maize + cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) (f)-potato-mentha + onion, maize + cowpea (f)-potato-spring maize, maize + cowpea (f)-gobhi sarson-summer moong (Vigna radiata), maizetoria (Brassica rapa) + gobhi sarson (Brassica napus)summer moong and maize + cowpea (f)-toria + gobhi sarson-summer moong and four irrigation schedules in sub plots: 0.75 IW/CPE, 1.0 IW/CPE, 1.25 IW/CPE and recommended schedule with three replications.
subpractice_description_raw: M-W: maize (Zea mays)-wheat (Triticum aestivum)
fert_subpractice_raw: Total fertilizer application was 125 kg N/ha, 60 kg P2O5/ha and 30 kg K2O/ha. One third of N and entire quantity of P2O5 and K2O were applied at the time of sowing.
weed_method_raw: Two hand weedings were given to control weeds.
chem_subpractice_raw: Seeds were treated with Bavistin 50 WP (carbendazim) @ 3 g/kg seed. Pre-emergence herbicide Stomp 30 EC (pendimethalin) was sprayed within 2 days of sowing. Decis 2.8 EC (deltamethrin) was sprayed to control maize borer.
irrig_subpractice_raw: The amount of irrigation water applied (mm) was calculated from the initial and the final flow meter readings divided by the area of the sub plot. First irrigation was applied before sowing and further irrigations were applied at the pre-tasseling, silking and grain filling stages.
out_exp_design: 3 replications
out_subindicator_description_raw: Net returns: Net returns were calculated by subtracting total variable cost from the gross returns.

exp_design: The experiment was laid out in split-plot design with seven crop sequences in main plots, viz. maize (Zea mays)-wheat (Triticum aestivum), maize-potato (Solanum tuberosum)mentha (Mentha arvensis) + onion (Allium cepa), maize + cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) (f)-potato-mentha + onion, maize + cowpea (f)-potato-spring maize, maize + cowpea (f)-gobhi sarson-summer moong (Vigna radiata), maizetoria (Brassica rapa) + gobhi sarson (Brassica napus)summer moong and maize + cowpea (f)-toria + gobhi sarson-summer moong and four irrigation schedules in sub plots: 0.75 IW/CPE, 1.0 IW/CPE, 1.25 IW/CPE and recommended schedule with three replications.
subpractice_description_raw: M+C(f)-P-SpM: maize  cowpea (f)-potato-spring maize
fert_subpractice_raw: Total fertilizer application was 125 kg N/ha, 60 kg P2O5/ha and 30 kg K2O/ha. One third of N and entire quantity of P2O5 and K2O were applied at the time of sowing.
weed_method_raw: Two hand weedings were given to control weeds.
chem_subpractice_raw: Seeds were treated with Bavistin 50 WP (carbendazim) @ 3 g/kg seed. Pre-emergence herbicide Stomp 30 EC (pendimethalin) was sprayed within 2 days of sowing. Decis 2.8 EC (deltamethrin) was sprayed to control maize borer.
irrig_subpractice_raw: The amount of irrigation water applied (mm) was calculated from the initial and the final flow meter readings divided by the area of the sub plot. First irrigation was applied before sowing and further irrigations were applied at the pre-tasseling, silking and grain filling stages.
out_exp_design: 3 replications
out_subindicator_raw: Apparent water productivity (kg/m3) of kharif maize
out_subindicator_description_raw: AWP (kg/m3) is the ratio of grain yield to irrigation water applied.

exp_design: Comparison of 5 land-use systems (natural forest, multistrata agroforest, cocoa agroforest, cassava monoculture, weedy grassland) across several villages near Pucallpa city, Peruvian Amazon. Four sampling plots per village (25 x 25 m); each plot sampled six times with monthly repetition (Macuya forest only four times). Insects collected using one Malaise trap, nine pitfall traps in a 5 x 5 m grid, and sweeping net zigzag transects (80 m) per plot, between 6:30-10:30 am, March-August 2009 and February-November 2010. Per Table 1, not all habitats occur in all villages.
time_raw: March to August 2009, and February to November 2010
subpractice_description_raw: primary natural forest (selectively logged 20+ yrs ago; closed canopy; 9 trees/25 m2; 95% ground shade) and ~20 yr old closed-canopy forest in Pimental
agrof_subpractice_raw: Natural forest selectively logged 20+ years, on the edges; trees, palms, shrubs, thick layer of fallen leaves and woody material; Closed canopy; tree density 9 trees/25 m2; 95% ground shade, several natural streams and small ponds of  standing water.
land_structure_subpractice_raw: Natural forest selectively logged 20+ years, on the edges; trees, palms, shrubs, thick layer of fallen leaves and woody material; Closed canopy; tree density 9 trees/25 m2; 95% ground shade, several natural streams and small ponds of  standing water.
out_exp_design: 12 plots of 25 x 25 m sampled (4 per village x 3 villages), plus Macuya forest plots. exp_design: Finger millet (var. Local) was planted either in sole stands (monocrop) or intercropped in alternate rows with D. intortum in experimental plots following the methodologies of Khan et al. (2006b). Finger millet was planted at a row-to-row distance of 60 cm and a plant-to-plant distance of 15 cm within a row. The layout comprised four large plots each measuring, 30 6 30 m where finger millet – D. intortum intercrop and the control were diagonally placed, with 2-m buffer strips between plots as described in Khan et al. (2006b). To facilitate sampling a method adapted from Khan et al. (2001) was used, with modifications, to create subplots within the established plots. Random-paired subplots of 8 6 8 m along perpendicular transect lines bisecting both treatment and control plots were demarcated with four replications in each plot.

exp_design: the entire field was divided into three blocks separated by a 1.5-m walkway and each block was subdivided into four plots each measuring 35 m × 41 m separated by earthen bunds (0.6 m wide and 0.3 m high). Four cropping system treatments referred to as scenarios (S) were designed based on different drivers of agricultural change (Table 2). The scenarios varied from each other in tillage, crop establishment, residue management, crop rotation and other management practices. Treatments referred to as scenarios 1–4 (S1–S4) were assigned to individual plots and replicated thrice in a randomized complete block design. Scenario details involving crop management and various field activities are provided in Tables 2 and 3, respectively.
time_raw: Crop production was distributed across the three seasons common in the country: Rabi, also called Boro (November to March); premonsoon Kharif-1, also called Aus (April to June); and monsoon Kharif-2, also called Aman (July to October). The trial began in Boro 2009–2010.
subpractice_description_raw: scenario 1: 1(business as usual–farmers practice): Rice (Boro)-fallow (Aus)-rice (Aman). This scenario represents current farmers’ practices of crop rotation, crop varieties and management (tillage and crop establishment, and residue), which were based on an on-farm survey conducted in 263 farmers’ fields during 2006–2008 in the neighboring area. Rice (Boro)–fallow (Aus)–rice (Aman) was the crop rotation because it is the predominant cropping pattern covering more than 80% of the cultivated area in the region. In both seasons (Boro and Aman), rice was grown by transplanting four to six seedlings per hill in puddled soil prepared by intensive wet tillage. Boro rice was irrigated but Aman rice was rainfed. Rice was harvested manually at or near ground level, leaving 5–10 cm standing biomass from the ground which was incorporated during land preparation of the next crop.

subpractice_description_raw: scenario 3: (best management practices with reduced tillage): rice (Boro)-fallow (Aus)-rice (Aman) crop rotation. time_raw: In Kapchorwa, 13 trials were established in 2016A and 10 in 2016B. Each farm hosted one unreplicated trial; hence, each farm represents one replicate.
subpractice_description_raw: Common bean and banana intercropping. No pruning variety improved: In both seasons, NABE 12C (released in 2005) was planted as the improved climbing bean variety. The experiment consisted of seven CS as the main plots: sole cropped maize without fertilizer (MZ), sole cropped maize with 92 kg top dressing N fertilizer per hectare (MZ + 92), sole cropped cowpea (CP), sole cropped pigeon pea (PP), intercrop of pigeon pea and maize (PP + MZ), intercrop of cowpea and maize (CP + MZ), and intercrop of pigeon pea and cowpea (PP + CP).
time_raw: A 2-year field experiment was conducted using a split plot design with three replications during the 2020–2021 and 2021–2022 CS (Figure 1).
subpractice_description_raw: PP+MZ: intercrop of pigeon pea and maize (PP + MZ). Deep bed
tillage_subpractice_raw: deep bed farming (DBF) All crop residues after harvest are returned to the deep bed as mulches.
intercrop_subpractice_raw: PP+MZ: intercrop of pigeon pea and maize (PP + MZ)
out_exp_design: All treatments were replicated three times.
out_subindicator_raw: sum of available nitrate and amonia
out_subindicator_description_raw: Soil samples were collected at depths of 0–20 cm in each plot using a soil auger, based on the simple random sampling during both years after harvest. The soil at the same depth of 0–20 cm was sampled from three points per plot and combined into composite samples. The soil samples were then air-dried for analysis of available P. Available P was determined using Mehlich-3 method (Anderson & Ingram, 1989),

The experiment consisted of seven CS as the main plots: sole cropped maize without fertilizer (MZ), sole cropped maize with 92 kg top dressing N fertilizer per hectare (MZ + 92), sole cropped cowpea (CP), sole cropped pigeon pea (PP), intercrop of pigeon pea and maize (PP + MZ), intercrop of cowpea and maize (CP + MZ), and intercrop of pigeon pea and cowpea (PP + CP).
time_raw: A 2-year field experiment was conducted using a split plot design with three replications during the 2020–2021 and 2021–2022 CS (Figure 1).
subpractice_description_raw: MZ+92: sole cropped maize with 92 kg top dressing N fertilizer per hectare (MZ + 92).Conventional tillage
fert_subpractice_raw: 92 kg top dressing N fertilizer per hectare (MZ + 92)
out_exp_design: NA
out_subindicator_raw: sum of available nitrate and amonia
out_subindicator_description_raw: Soil samples were collected at depths of 0–20 cm in each plot using a soil auger, based on the simple random sampling during both years after harvest. The soil at the same depth of 0–20 cm was sampled from three points per plot and combined into composite samples. The soil samples were then air-dried for analysis of available P. Available P was determined using Mehlich-3 method (Anderson & Ingram, 1989),
